newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan hog markets reopen after epidemic.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan hog markets reopen after epidemic.

text.p: Taiwan on Saturday reopened hog trading at 19 of the island's 22 major wholesale centres which were closed for five days as troops slaughtered pigs infected with highly contagious foot and mouth disease.
Several county hog trading associations held parties on Saturday to give citizens a free lunch of pork as a promotion to attract back consumers.

State television showed dozens of people in the central city of Taichung lining up and struggling to get a free lunch box of pig's trotter and noodles, until staff ran out after handing out several hundred.
"If it is cooked it can be eaten. There is nothing to be afraid of," a male citizen said on televison.
Officials took the lead in eating pork at the parties.
"Starting today, don't be afraid, let's eat pork together," said Taichung's acting mayor Lin Hsueh-cheng, who was eating pig's trotter with a smile.
Officials said shoppers can ask pork vendors to show a certificate proving the pork they are buying is not contaminated by the disease.
"All the pork now available in markets is fit for human consumption," an official at the provincial government's sanitary department said.
The fast-moving foot and mouth epidemic spread to more than 1,000 breeding centres, from nine when the outbreak was confirmed on March 20, officials said on Friday.

The mass slaughter of pigs -- healthy or otherwise -- at all farms struck by the deadly contagion continued with experts reporting that over 886,000 would have to be destroyed, the cabinet's Council of Agriculture said.

As of late on Friday, the virus had been detected on 1,008 of Taiwan's 25,000 hog farms, though only 160,315 pigs had been slaughtered, official statistics showed. Some 46,500 pigs had died of the disease, officials said.
Industry sources quoted by the ruling Nationalist Party on Wednesday estimated that about 15 percent of Taiwan's 11 million swine -- or 1.6 million animals -- would be affected directly.
The farm council banned all pork exports after confirming the outbreak on March 20.

The crisis threatened to slow the island's gathering economic recovery, battered the stock market and threatened tens of thousands of jobs in the huge feedlot and meat-packing sectors, which employ 700,000.

The crisis reduced local demand for animal feed, forcing cancellations of tenders for nearly 200,000 tonnes of corn and soy since March 20 and, on Friday, the first voiding of a contract -- one to import 25,000 tonnes of corn.
Taiwan corn buyers estimated the crisis would slash the island's feed corn imports by about one-fifth.

A Reuters survey of five major grain importers found that all expected significant reductions in corn imports, with most estimating the downturn at about 1.2 million tonnes of the island's annual imports of 6.5 million tonnes.
